title: As above, so below — what the line actually says
desc: The most quoted sentence in esotericism, traced to its source: medieval Latin translating Arabic, a simile with a purpose clause, and the Victorian compression that turned an instruction into a slogan.
tldr: Four words that almost nobody has read in the original — because there is no original. The line comes from the Emerald Tablet, first attested in Arabic in the eighth or ninth century, reaching Europe in Latin translation. What the Latin says is not a cosmic slogan but an operative claim: what is below is like what is above, and the reverse, for the purpose of accomplishing one thing. The crisp modern epigram was popularised in the age of Blavatsky.
body:
If you have encountered one sentence from this tradition, it is this one. It is printed on tarot boxes, tattooed, quoted in films and attributed, confidently, to Hermes Trismegistus in ancient Egypt. Almost every part of that sentence is wrong. What remains, once the errors are cleared away, is more interesting than the myth.

Where the line comes from

It is not in the Corpus Hermeticum. It comes from the Emerald Tablet, a short text of a dozen lines whose earliest surviving witness is Arabic: it appears embedded in the Kitab sirr al-khaliqa (the Book of the Secret of Creation), a work attributed to Balinas and dated by most scholars to the eighth or ninth century CE. There is no Greek original, no Egyptian original, no tablet of emerald and no verified discovery. What we have is a text that enters the historical record already in Arabic and reaches Latin Europe through translation in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries.

What the Latin actually says

The medieval Latin vulgate runs, in our working translation: “That which is below is like that which is above, and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing.” Three things are worth noticing, and all three vanish in the popular version.

First, it is a simile, not an identity. Like, not the same as. The levels answer each other; they are not each other.

Second, it is symmetrical and stated twice. Below is like above, and above is like below. The doubling is doing work: influence runs both ways, which is precisely what makes a practitioner's action meaningful rather than decorative.

Third — and this is the part that disappears entirely — the sentence has a purpose clause. To accomplish the miracles of the one thing. The correspondence is not stated for its own sake. It is stated as the reason a particular operation can work. This is an operator's sentence, written to justify a procedure, not a poster.

How it became a slogan

The tight four-word epigram in English — as above, so below — belongs to the era of modern occultism. Theosophical and Hermetic-revival writers of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries compressed the medieval line into a maxim, and the Kybalion of 1908 then enshrined it as one of seven “principles” alongside six others the medieval text knows nothing about. The compression is not a translation error. It is a genre change: from a technical premise inside a recipe to a piece of portable wisdom.

The manuscript tradition also varies on the exact Latin wording, which is a useful reminder in itself — the line most people treat as eternal has textual variants, like any other medieval text.

What the claim is actually doing

Read as its authors read it, the sentence answers a practical question: why should working on this substance, in this vessel, change anything that matters? The answer is that the levels of reality are structurally related, so a change effected at one level is not isolated. That is why the Tablet goes on to describe separation, ascent and descent, and the joining of the powers of above and below — a procedure, not a meditation.

You do not have to accept the metaphysics to use the observation, and this is where the line earns its long life. Take it as a claim about systems: the pattern in your week and the pattern in your work are not two unrelated things; a change in the smaller system shows up in the larger one, and the reverse. That reading is honest — provided you say plainly that it is a modern application and not what a thirteenth-century alchemist meant.

The line is not ancient Egyptian. It is not a slogan. It is a medieval Latin translation of an Arabic text, making a symmetrical claim about levels of reality — in order to accomplish something. The purpose clause is the part worth keeping.
facts: The Emerald Tablet, not the Corpus Hermeticum
Arabic, 8th–9th c. CE, in the Kitab sirr al-khaliqa
None known; no manuscript, no citation, no fragment
Popularised in the Theosophical era; codified by the Kybalion (1908)
faq: No — it is genuinely old, just not as old or as Egyptian as the myth says. Eighth-century Arabic is a serious antiquity. What is invented is the provenance story: the emerald slab, the tomb, the hand of Hermes.
Does the Corpus Hermeticum say anything similar?

It says related things in its own words — the cosmos as an image of God, the human as an image of the cosmos — but the famous sentence is not there. If someone quotes it as Corpus Hermeticum, they are repeating a chain of citation nobody checked.

Yes, if you use it honestly. Quote it as a medieval Latin line translating Arabic, keep the purpose clause, and mark your own application as yours. That costs one sentence and buys the difference between a claim and a decoration.
sources: Julius Ruska, Tabula Smaragdina (1926) — the foundational study of the Arabic and Latin transmission.
Kevin van Bladel, The Arabic Hermes (Oxford UP, 2009) — on the Arabic milieu and the Balinas material.
